proposal.problem: The IKU Computer Club hands out participation certificates for its workshops and events as plain PDF or printed files. According to the club's events organization coordinator, the club issues about 150 to 200 certificates per semester, and a single workshop or large event gives out 50 to 70 certificates to attendees. These files are made from a shared template, so anyone with a PDF editor can change a name, a date or an event title in a few minutes, and the result looks identical to a genuine certificate. When a company asks whether a certificate is real, the club has to search by hand through the Excel files and Google Drive folders linked to that event to find the person's name; the club reports that this takes about 1 to 2 days before they can reply. Once a board graduates, these files are easily lost. As a result, certificate holders cannot prove that their certificate is real, verifiers either trust the file blindly or ignore it, and the club cannot withdraw a certificate that was issued by mistake. The club has no budget for a paid certificate platform, so the solution must run at zero cost. The problem is not storing the file, which the club already does, but giving third parties an independent proof that the club issued it and has not revoked it.
proposal.mission: CertiChain lets an IKU student club issue event certificates whose authenticity anyone can check in seconds. The event organiser issues certificates from a simple dashboard; each certificate's fingerprint is recorded on a public blockchain. Every certificate holder gets a PDF with a QR code, and any verifier can confirm it is genuine and not revoked without contacting the club or trusting a central server.
proposal.outcome: Once CertiChain exists, a certificate holder can send a single link that proves their certificate is genuine, a verifier can check it in under ten seconds without e-mailing anyone, and the club can revoke a wrong certificate publicly, even after the board that issued it has graduated.

entities.def: A record that a named participant attended a specific club event, issued as a JSON-LD document and PDF whose SHA-256 hash is stored on chain.
A club wallet address authorised by the contract owner to issue and revoke certificates.
A workshop, bootcamp or competition run by the club, with a title, date and organiser.
The certificate holder: an attendee identified off chain by name and e-mail; on chain only through a salted hash.
An on-chain record that a certificate is no longer valid, with the time and the issuer who revoked it.

proposal.techWhy: JSON-LD 1.1 contexts give each certificate a machine-readable format that follows the W3C Verifiable Credentials data model, so other systems can read it, and its canonical form is what we hash. PROV-O describes who issued the certificate, for which event and when, so the provenance chain is explicit. SHACL shapes check every certificate before it is issued, so a malformed certificate never reaches the chain; RDFLib with pySHACL-style validation runs those checks in our test suite. Stable IRI practice gives every certificate a permanent verification URL that the QR code points to. Outside the semantic stack we use Solidity with OpenZeppelin AccessControl, Hardhat for testing and deployment, ethers.js in the browser, React for the pages and Node.js for the PDF and QR service.

goals.goal: Any verifier can confirm that a certificate is genuine and not revoked without contacting the club
goals.why: This is the mission itself: if it holds, the problem of unverifiable certificates is solved.

goals.goal: The registry contract issues, revokes and verifies certificates and is deployed on Sepolia
goals.why: Without the contract there is no tamper-proof record to check against.

goals.goal: The organiser can issue a whole event's certificates from the dashboard in one batch
goals.why: If issuing is harder than the current template, the club will not use the system.

goals.goal: Every certificate follows one JSON-LD format and passes the SHACL shape before issue
goals.why: A single checked format keeps hashes reproducible and certificates readable by others.

goals.goal: No work goes into features outside the four areas, and no personal data is written on chain
goals.why: Keeps a one-term team effort focused and keeps the project KVKK-safe.

proposal.spec: The system has three parts. A CertificateRegistry smart contract on Sepolia keeps a mapping from a certificate hash to its issuer, issue time and revocation status; only wallets holding the ISSUER role may call issue or revoke, and anyone may call verify for free. The issuer dashboard lets an event organiser connect MetaMask, enter event details and upload a CSV of participants; the certificate service builds one JSON-LD certificate per participant, validates it against the SHACL shape, salts and hashes it with SHA-256, and the dashboard submits all hashes in one batch transaction. The service then produces a PDF per participant with a QR code linking to the verification page. The verification page, needing no wallet, reads the certificate ID from the link or recomputes the hash from an uploaded file, queries the contract through a public RPC endpoint and shows Valid, Revoked or Not found, with the issuing club and date. Names and student numbers stay off chain.

scenarios.text: Given a certificate issued by the club for the Git workshop, when a verifier scans its QR code, then the page shows Valid with the club name and issue date.
Given a certificate PDF whose participant name was edited after issue, when a verifier uploads it, then the recomputed hash is not found and the page shows Not found.
Given a wallet without the ISSUER role, when it calls issue on the contract, then the transaction reverts and no certificate is recorded.
Given a certificate that the organiser has revoked, when a verifier checks it, then the page shows Revoked with the revocation date instead of Valid.
Given an empty CSV attendance file, when the organiser starts issuing, then the dashboard stops with an error and sends no transaction.

proposal.activity: 1. The organiser runs the event and exports the attendance list as CSV. 2. The organiser connects MetaMask to the dashboard; if the wallet has no ISSUER role, the flow stops with an error. 3. The organiser enters event details and uploads the CSV; if the file is empty or malformed, the dashboard rejects it. 4. The service builds and SHACL-validates one certificate per row; invalid rows are listed for correction. 5. The dashboard sends one batch transaction; on failure nothing is recorded and the organiser may retry. 6. PDFs with QR codes are generated and e-mailed or downloaded. 7. A verifier opens the QR link; the page queries the contract and branches to Valid, Revoked or Not found.
proposal.sequence: Organiser → Dashboard: upload CSV and event details. Dashboard → Certificate service: build certificates. Certificate service → SHACL validator: validate each; validator → service: report. Service → Dashboard: list of hashes. Dashboard → MetaMask: request signature for issueBatch(hashes). MetaMask → Registry contract: transaction. Contract → Dashboard: CertificateIssued events. Dashboard → Service: generate PDFs. Verifier → Verification page: open QR link with certificate ID. Page → Public RPC → Registry contract: verify(hash). Contract → Page: issuer, date, revoked flag. Page → Verifier: result.

proposal.classModel: CertificateRegistry (contract): owner: address; certificates: mapping(bytes32 => CertificateRecord); functions issue(bytes32), issueBatch(bytes32[]), revoke(bytes32), verify(bytes32) returns (issuer, issuedAt, revoked, revokedAt); uses OpenZeppelin AccessControl with ISSUER_ROLE. CertificateRecord (struct): issuer: address; issuedAt: uint64; revoked: bool; revokedAt: uint64. Certificate (off chain, JSON-LD): id: URI; event: Event; participant: Participant; issuedBy: Issuer; issuedOn: date; salt: string; hash: bytes32. Event: title, date, organiser. Participant: name, email (off chain only). Issuer: clubName, wallet address. Relations: an Event has many Certificates; a Certificate belongs to one Participant and one Issuer; a CertificateRecord stores the hash of exactly one Certificate.

proposal.model_Data: Class diagram: CertificateRegistry holds a mapping from bytes32 hash to CertificateRecord (issuer, issuedAt, revoked, revokedAt). Off chain, Certificate links Event, Participant and Issuer; only its salted SHA-256 hash crosses to the chain.
proposal.model_Security: State machine for a certificate hash: Unknown → Issued (issue by ISSUER_ROLE only) → Revoked (revoke by ISSUER_ROLE only). Revoked is final; issuing an existing hash is refused; any call from a wallet without the role is refused in every state.
proposal.model_Interaction: Sequence diagram: Organiser uploads CSV to Dashboard; Dashboard asks the service to build and validate certificates; MetaMask signs issueBatch; the contract emits events; Verifier opens the QR link; the page calls verify through a public RPC and shows the result.
proposal.model_User_interface: Mockups for three screens: dashboard event form with CSV upload and batch preview; certificate PDF layout with QR code; verification page with a large green Valid, orange Revoked or red Not found result and the issuer details below.
proposal.chainDesign:
We use the Ethereum Sepolia testnet so the system costs nothing and is still public and independent of us; the contract could later move to a cheap layer-2 such as Polygon without changes. A Solidity CertificateRegistry contract, using OpenZeppelin AccessControl, stores only the SHA-256 hash of each salted JSON-LD certificate with its issuer and time, plus a revocation flag; verifying is a free read call. A blockchain is needed because the verifier must not have to trust the club or our server: a normal database run by the club could be edited or disappear when the board graduates, while the on-chain record is append-only, timestamped and publicly readable by anyone. Personal data stays off chain to respect KVKK.

Link to the course chapters. Chapter 1: the trust argument above is the problem a public, tamper-evident ledger solves, and Sepolia lets us use it without real money. Chapters 2 and 6: an issuer sends one transaction, issueBatch, that records many certificate hashes at once, so the cost and the waiting time are shared by the whole event. Chapter 4: the certificate hash is a commitment; the salt keeps the hash from being guessed and the contract never sees the certificate itself. Chapters 7 and 8: only wallets with the issuer role may write, and each write is authorised by a digital signature made in the issuer's MetaMask wallet, so the registry cannot be changed by anyone else. Verification needs no wallet, because it only reads the chain. Bitcoin-specific topics (Script, UTXOs, running Bitcoin Core) are not used, since Ethereum accounts and smart contracts replace them; we state this choice on purpose.

risks.risk: Sepolia faucet limits or RPC outages slow down testing
risks.mitigation: Develop on a local Hardhat network, keep two RPC providers and request test ETH early.

risks.risk: The customer club is not available for the trial in December
risks.mitigation: Agree the trial date at the first meeting; fall back to another club event or a mock event with real club members.

risks.risk: Smart-contract bug lets a non-issuer write or blocks revocation
risks.mitigation: Use audited OpenZeppelin AccessControl, aim for 90% test coverage and review every contract change.

risks.risk: Team members overloaded by capstone and other courses
risks.mitigation: Keep scope to the four areas, every module has a second member, and weekly 30-minute check-ins.

risks.risk: Personal data accidentally leaks on chain
risks.mitigation: Only salted hashes on chain; DoD criterion and test S8 check every release.
